stem: When preparing statements from incomplete records, the **opening capital** is usually found from …

options.rationale: Correct: opening assets less opening liabilities.

options.content: the summary of the bank account for the year
options.rationale: The bank summary gives receipts, payments and the closing bank balance.
This gives credit sales.

options.content: the income statement for the year
options.rationale: The income statement gives profit, not capital.

explanation: With no capital account, opening capital = opening assets − opening liabilities.

stem: A trader's revenue was US\$36,000. All goods are sold at a mark-up of 20% on cost. What was the gross profit?

options.rationale: This treats the mark-up as a margin (20% of selling price).
This is the cost of sales, not the gross profit.
This divides by 80, as if the figure were a 20% margin converted the wrong way.

explanation: With a 20% mark-up, selling price = 120% of cost, so gross profit = 36,000 × 20/120 = 6,000.

stem: Revenue was US\$54,000 and the gross profit margin is 30%. What was the cost of sales?

options.rationale: This is the gross profit.
This treats 30% as a mark-up on cost.
Cost of sales cannot be more than revenue when there is a gross profit.

explanation: Margin is a percentage of revenue: gross profit 16,200, cost of sales 37,800.

stem: Cost of sales was US\$42,000 and the rate of inventory turnover was 6 times. Opening inventory was US\$6,400. What was the closing inventory?

options.rationale: This is the average inventory, not the closing inventory.
Half the opening inventory has been deducted from the average instead of using 2 × average − opening.
Opening inventory has been added instead of deducted.
Correct: average 7,000; closing = 2 × 7,000 − 6,400.

explanation: Average inventory = 42,000 ÷ 6 = 7,000. Opening + closing = 14,000, so closing = 14,000 − 6,400 = 7,600.
hints: Average inventory = cost of sales ÷ turnover.

stem: The bank summary of a trader with incomplete records shows a payment of US\$3,500 for a new display cabinet. How is it treated?

options.content: Charged as an expense in the income statement
options.rationale: Only depreciation on the cabinet is an expense.
The cabinet is for the business, not the owner.

options.content: Added to purchases in cost of sales
options.rationale: Purchases are goods for resale; the cabinet is not for resale.

options.content: Added to the cost of non-current assets
options.rationale: Correct: it is capital expenditure.

explanation: A payment for a non-current asset is capital expenditure; it is depreciated over its life.

stem: A flood damaged part of Tatenda's inventory on 31 December 2025. Revenue for 2025 was US\$25,000; goods are sold at a mark-up of 25%. Opening inventory was US\$3,100 and purchases US\$21,600. Undamaged inventory was valued at US\$3,800. What was the cost of the inventory destroyed?

options.rationale: This uses a 25% margin (cost of sales 18,750) instead of a 25% mark-up.
Correct: cost of sales 20,000; closing inventory should be 4,700; 4,700 − 3,800.
This is the closing inventory that should be held, not the amount destroyed.
This is the undamaged inventory left, not the inventory destroyed.

stem: A student's statement of financial position prepared from incomplete records does not balance: net assets are US\$4,200 lower than closing capital. Which omission could explain this?

options.content: A trade payable of US\$4,200 left out of current liabilities
options.rationale: This would make net assets too high, not too low.

options.content: Drawings of US\$4,200 left out of the capital section
options.rationale: Correct: capital is overstated by the drawings omitted.

options.content: Capital introduced of US\$4,200 left out of the capital section
options.rationale: This would make closing capital too low, not too high.

options.content: Cash sales of US\$4,200 left out of revenue
options.rationale: Leaving out revenue would make capital lower, not higher.

explanation: Closing capital = opening capital + profit − drawings. Forgetting drawings makes capital too high by exactly the drawings.
hints: Which side of the statement is too large?

stem: Expenses owing at the year end that were found when reconstructing an expense account appear in the statement of financial position as …

options.rationale: Prepaid expenses are current assets; amounts owing are liabilities.
Capital is changed only through profit, drawings and capital introduced.
Correct: they are amounts the business still owes (other payables).
Expenses owing are payable within a year.

explanation: Accrued expenses are current liabilities; prepaid expenses are current assets.

stem: A mark-up of 25% on cost is the same as a gross profit margin of 20% on selling price.
explanation: True. Cost 100, gross profit 25, selling price 125: 25/125 = 20%.

stem: Cambridge 0452 examines the preparation of financial statements from incomplete records for service and manufacturing businesses as well as trading businesses.
explanation: False. The Cambridge syllabus restricts incomplete records to trading businesses.

stem: Match each figure needed for the statements with the working that provides it.

left.content: Revenue when sales records are lost

right.content: Mark-up applied to cost of sales

explanation: Each working supplies one missing figure; together they give everything needed for both statements.
hints: Think about which account each figure would have been posted to.

stem: Complete the statements for a trader whose mark-up is 50%.

payload.template: If cost of sales is US\$30,000, gross profit is US\$ {{blank:a}} and revenue is US\$ {{blank:b}}. The gross profit margin is {{blank:c}} %.

hints: Mark-up is on cost; margin is on selling price.

stem: Sipho sells all goods at a mark-up of 40%. Opening inventory was US\$4,850, credit purchases US\$39,200, cash purchases US\$1,600 and closing inventory US\$5,350. Calculate his revenue for the year.
hints: Find cost of sales first, then add the mark-up.

stem: Thandeka's revenue for 2025 was US\$72,500 and her gross profit margin was 28%. Inventory was US\$8,900 at 1 January 2025 and US\$7,650 at 31 December 2025. Calculate her purchases for 2025.
explanation: Cost of sales = 72,500 × 72% = 52,200. Purchases = 52,200 + 7,650 − 8,900 = 50,950. Getting the inventories the wrong way round gives 53,450.
workedSolution: 1. Cost of sales = 72,500 × 72% = 52,200. Purchases = 52,200 + 7,650 − 8,900 = 50,950. Getting the inventories the wrong way round gives 53,450.
hints: Cost of sales = opening inventory + purchases − closing inventory. Rearrange for purchases.

stem: At 1 January 2025 a trader's fixtures cost US\$12,500. During the year the bank summary shows a payment of US\$3,000 for more fixtures. Depreciation is 20% of the cost of fixtures held at 31 December. Calculate the depreciation for 2025.
Explain why a trader's bank manager may want a full income statement rather than just a profit figure found from the change in capital.

points.description: The income statement shows revenue, gross profit and each expense
So the manager can judge how the profit was made / whether it is sustainable / the ability to repay a loan

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A profit figure alone does not show where it came from. The income statement shows sales, gross profit and expenses, so the manager can judge whether the business earns enough, steadily, to repay a loan.

explanation: Lenders need detail to assess risk.

stem: Farai always sells at a mark-up of 30%. His actual gross profit this year is lower than 30% of cost of sales would give. Suggest **three** possible reasons.

points.description: Theft or loss of inventory / cash takings
Goods taken for own use not recorded as drawings
Goods sold at reduced prices (discounts, damaged or old stock) / cost prices rose without selling prices changing / errors in inventory count

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Goods or cash may have been stolen; Farai may have taken goods for his family without recording them; or some goods were sold at reduced prices because they were damaged or slow-moving.

explanation: A shortfall against a fixed mark-up points to losses, unrecorded drawings or price changes.
hints: Anything that reduces revenue or increases cost of sales without being recorded.

stem: Chipo runs a cash-only stationery kiosk in Masvingo and sells everything at a mark-up of 35%. For 2025: inventory at 1 January US\$3,640; purchases US\$28,460; inventory at 31 December US\$4,100. She banked US\$33,290 of takings and paid US\$1,450 of expenses in cash from the takings. She took no drawings. She suspects that an assistant has been taking cash.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the revenue Chipo should have received.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the cash that appears to be missing.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest **three** controls Chipo could introduce to reduce the risk of cash going missing.

points.description: Use a till or numbered receipts for every sale and check them against cash
Pay expenses by bank transfer or petty cash imprest, not from takings; surprise cash counts / separate duties

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Bank the takings every day without paying anything out of them; issue a numbered receipt for every sale and reconcile receipts with cash each evening; pay expenses from a separate petty cash float.

parts.explanation: Controls should make every sale recorded and every dollar traceable.

explanation: Cost of sales 28,000; expected revenue 37,800; accounted for 34,740; missing 3,060.
